It is permissible for ﴿on the day the sky will be﴾ to be linked to the verb (ta'ruju, "ascend") [in the preceding verse], and it is also permissible for it to be linked to (yawaddu al-mujrimu, "the guilty one would wish"), being placed before it for emphasis on mentioning the day. In that case, His saying ﴿on the day the sky will be like molten metal﴾ is the beginning of a new statement. A sentence that is made the beginning of a statement is treated as a comprehensive substitute (badal al-ishtimal, a substitute that encompasses what precedes it) for the sentence ﴿and no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend﴾, because the absence of questioning is caused by the severity of the terror, and among what that terror encompasses is that the one who turns away would wish to ransom himself from that punishment.

Al-muhl (molten metal) means the dregs of oil. The meaning is the comparison of the sky, in the dissolving of its parts, to oil. This is like His saying in Surat al-Rahman ﴿and it became red like tanned leather﴾ [al-Rahman: 37].

Al-ihn (wool) means dyed wool. It has been said that it means dyed in general, and it has been said that it means dyed in various colours, and this is the view adopted by al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) and al-Zamakhshari. Zuhayr said:

"The crumbs of dyed wool in every abode they alighted at were like the seeds of the al-Fana plant, unbroken."

Al-Fana, with a short alif, is a seed in the desert, called ʿinab al-thaʿlab (fox grapes), and it has colours: some of it is green, some yellow, and some red. Al-ʿihnah is a tree in the desert that has red blossoms.

The point of resemblance with wool is the scattering of the parts, as it came in the verse of al-Qari'ah ﴿and the mountains will be like carded wool﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 5]. The singling out of wool for mention is to complete the resemblance, because the mountains have colours. He, exalted is He, said ﴿and among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of varying colours﴾ [Fatir: 27]. The sky and the mountains will be in this state only when the cohesion of their parts is dissolved at the passing away of this world and the transition to the world of the Hereafter.

The meaning of ﴿and no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend﴾ is that, because of the severity of the terror that befalls people, one who sees his intimate friend in distress and hardship will not have leisure to ask him about his condition, because he is occupied with something else. Thus the object of (yas'alu, "asks") is omitted, as it is evident from the context and from His saying (yubassarunahum, "they will be shown to them"). That is, intimate friends will see the states of their intimate friends in distress, so no intimate friend will ask after another. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

[Page 160]

"Every intimate friend I had hoped for said: 'I will not distract you, for I am busy with myself regarding you.'"

Al-hamim means the close friend, the companion.

Al-Jumhur read (yas'alu) with a fatha on the ya', in the active voice. Abu Ja'far and al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, read it with a damma on the ya', in the passive voice. Then the meaning is: no intimate friend will be asked about an intimate friend, with the preposition omitted.

The position of (yubassarunahum, "they will be shown to them") is an explanatory resumptive clause (al-istinaf al-bayani, a new sentence answering an implied question) to dispel the possibility that it might occur to the listener that close friends do not see one another that day, because everyone is occupied. So it is answered that they will be shown their close ones, so that they see what they are suffering of punishment, and so they will be given punishment upon punishment.

It is also permissible for the clause (yubassarunahum) to be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). That is, no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend while every intimate friend sees his intimate friend, and it is said to him: "Look at what so-and-so is suffering."

(Yubassarunahum) is the present tense of basarahu bi-l-amr, meaning he made him see it, that is, made him a viewer of it. Its origin is yubassaruna bihim, so the preposition was dropped and the verb was made to take a direct object.

The two pronouns refer to (hamimun, "intimate friend") in the nominative and to (hamiman, "intimate friend") in the accusative. That is, every intimate friend sees his intimate friend. The two pronouns are plural, in view of the generality of (hamimun) and (hamiman) in a negative context.

(Yawaddu) means he loves, that is, he wishes. This may happen through a thought that comes to his mind on seeing the punishment, or through a statement that issues from him, like His saying ﴿and the disbeliever will say: "Would that I were dust!"﴾ [al-Naba': 40]. This is the apparent meaning, that is, the disbeliever will cry out on that day and say: "I would ransom myself from the punishment with my sons, my spouse and my kin," and this will be a disgrace for him that day before his family.

Al-mujrim is one who commits a jurm, which is a great sin, namely disbelief, because at the beginning of the mission people were of two kinds: disbelievers and obedient believers.

(Yawma'idhin, "that day") is the same as ﴿the day the sky will be like molten metal﴾. If His saying ﴿the day the sky will be﴾ is linked to (yawaddu), then His saying (yawma'idhin) is an emphasis of ﴿the day the sky will be like molten metal﴾. If it is linked to His saying (ta'ruju al-malaikatu, "the angels ascend"), then His saying (yawma'idhin) conveys that this day is the day when the guilty one would wish to ransom himself from punishment with those mentioned after it.

[Page 161]

(Law, "would that") is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), so what follows it is in the position of the object of (yawaddu), that is: the day of ransoming oneself from punishment with his sons, and so on to the end of the verse.

Al-Jumhur read (yawmi'idhin) with a kasra on the mim of (yawm), in the genitive, by the annexation of (adhab, "punishment") to it. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha on the mim, as its being built on the annexation of (yawm) to (idh), which is an indeclinable noun. Both readings are permissible.

Al-iftida' means giving a ransom (fida'), which is what is given as a substitute for rescue from a consequence. From it is His saying ﴿and if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85] in al-Baqarah, and His saying ﴿even if he were to ransom himself with it﴾ in Al 'Imran. The meaning is: would that he ransom himself. The preposition (bi-) after the root of ransom introduces the substitute given, so the meaning of (bi-) is substitution.

The meaning of (min, "from") is figurative origin, since the verb (yaftadi, "ransoms himself") is taken to mean (yatakhallasu, "frees himself"). (Sahibatuhu, "his spouse") means his wife.

Al-fasilah (kin) means the nearest relatives of the tribe, and they are the relatives who are separated from one, that is, those who are extracted from one. So it includes fathers and mothers. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Ashhab said: "I asked Malik about the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿and his kin who shelters him﴾, and he said: 'It is his mother.'" Meaning: the father is understood from it by the way of implication (lahn al-khitab, what is understood from the implied sense of the speech). So the nearest kin are fully mentioned, both explicitly and by implication. As for the well-known interpretation, al-fasilah indicates the fathers by the wording, and the mothers are derived by the implication of the discourse.

The relatives have been arranged according to the degree of natural inclination towards them in common custom, because natural inclination arises from constant companionship and frequent association.

He did not mention the two parents, because they are included in al-fasilah, for the sake of brevity.

Al-iwa' means gathering together and taking refuge. He, exalted is He, said ﴿he took his brother to himself﴾ [Yusuf: 69], and He said ﴿I will take refuge in a mountain﴾ [Hud: 43].

As for (allati tu'wihi, "who shelters him"): if it means the tribe, then al-iwa' is a figurative usage for protection and support, that is, and despite that he would ransom himself with them, knowing that they will not avail him anything that day. If it means the mother, then al-iwa' is in its literal sense, with regard to the past tense and the present-tense form, to bring the state vividly before the mind, like His saying ﴿and Allah is He who sends the winds, so they raise clouds﴾ [Fatir: 9]. That is: he would wish to ransom himself with his mother, despite the strength of his attachment to her, since she used to shelter him. So the choice of the word (fasilatihi, "his kin") and the verb (tu'wihi, "shelters him") here is part of the concision and inimitability of the Qur'an, to include all these meanings.

([wa-man fi al-ardi jami'an, "and all who are on earth"]) is coordinated with (banihi, "his sons"), that is: and he would ransom himself with whoever is on earth, that is, whoever belongs to him on earth of what is dear to him, such as intimate friends, relatives, and precious wealth, which people are usually stingy about giving and eager to keep, in the manner of His saying ﴿so there will not be accepted from any of them the earth full of gold, even if he ransomed himself with it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91].

The relative pronoun (man) is used to give precedence to the rational over the non-rational, because among them are intimate friends.

(Thumma, "then") in His saying (thumma yunjihi, "then it would save him") indicates a sequence of rank, that is: he would wish to give all that and to be saved from the punishment by the ransom. So being saved from punishment is the most important thing for the guilty one in his longing. The prominent pronoun in His saying (yunjihi) refers to the ransoming that is understood from (yaftadi, "ransoms himself"), in the manner of His saying ﴿be just, that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8].

The clause coordinated with (thumma) is the consequence of the longing, so the apparent expectation was that it would be coordinated with (fa, "so"), which is the more common usage in such cases, as in His saying ﴿they wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike﴾ [al-Nisa': 89], and His saying ﴿they wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam: 9]. But here He changed from coordinating with (fa) to coordinating with (thumma), to indicate the intensity of the guilty one's concern for salvation by any means.

The object of (yunjihi) is omitted, and it is indicated by His saying (min 'adhabi yawma'idhin, "from the punishment of that day").

(Kalla, "No!") is a particle of repulsion and nullification of a preceding statement, and it is not free of having a statement mentioned after it. Here it serves to nullify what the longing of the guilty one entertains in his soul, and it takes the place of a statement, because Allah is aware of it, or to nullify what is uttered of wishing for that. He, exalted is He, said ﴿and the disbeliever will say: "Would that I were dust!"﴾ [al-Naba': 40]. Do you not see that He expressed that statement by the longing in His saying ﴿that day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth would be levelled over them﴾ [al-Nisa': 42], that is, that they would become part of its dust.

So the implied meaning is: it is said to him, "No!" That is: no ransoming and no salvation.

The sentence (﴿indeed it is a blazing fire﴾) is an explanatory resumptive clause, arising from what the particle (kalla, "No!") conveys of nullification. The pronoun of (innaha, "indeed it") refers to what the guilty one sees before him of the sight of Hell. So He informed that this is a blazing fire (la?a). Since (la?a) is accompanied by the feminine alif, the pronoun is made feminine in accordance with the feminine gender of the predicate, and its subject is followed by descriptive attributes. The purpose is an indirect allusion that it has been prepared for him, that is: it will burn you and strip away your limbs. And what the indirect allusion pointed to is stated explicitly in His saying ﴿calling him who turned his back and withdrew, and gathered and hoarded﴾, that is: it calls you, O one who turned his back on the call to monotheism and withdrew from it and was concerned only with gathering wealth.

So the particle (inna, "indeed") is for emphasis of the indirect allusive meaning of the statement, not for the report that what he sees is a blazing fire, since that is not a matter open to doubt. (La?a) is the predicate of (inna).

It is also permissible for the pronoun of (innaha) to be the pronoun of the matter (dhamir al-qissah, the pronoun of the situation or affair), that is: indeed your situation and affair is a blazing fire. Then (la?a) would be the subject.

Al-Jumhur read (nazza'atun, "stripping away") in the nominative, so it is a second predicate of (inna) if the pronoun is taken to refer to the fire that is seen, or it is a predicate of (la?a) if the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter and (la?a) is taken as the subject.

Hafs read it in the accusative as a circumstantial state, so according to Hafs's reading it is necessary that the pronoun is not the pronoun of the matter. The indirect allusion is the same, and the particle (inna) is either for emphasis directed at the allusive meaning, as already explained, or merely for giving special importance to the sentence that follows it, because sentences opening with the pronoun of the matter are among the statements given special importance.

(La?a) is a proper noun transferred from the noun meaning "blaze", and it was made a proper noun for (jahannam, "Hell"). Its alif is the alif of feminine gender. Its original form was la?an, on the pattern of fatan, with tanwin, as a common noun for the blaze of fire. The common noun was transferred to become a proper noun for one specific member of its kind, and so it was given the feminine alif, as an indication, by that change, of its transfer to the status of a proper noun.

The Arabs sometimes introduce a change to a word that is not a proper noun when they transfer it to the status of a proper noun, as they named Shams with a damma on the shin, transferred from Shams with a fatha on the shin, as Ibn Jinni said in explaining the verse of Ta'abbata Sharran:

"Indeed I am one who sends forth my praise, aiming it at the son of the uncle of truth, Shums ibn Malik."

It is not a proper noun by dominance, since it is neither definite nor annexed. Because it combines being a proper noun and being feminine, it is prohibited from taking tanwin. So you do not say la?an with tanwin unless you mean the common kind of blaze, and you do not say al-la?a unless you mean a particular blaze. But if you mean the name of Hell, you say la?a with the feminine alif, without tanwin and without the definite article.

(Nazza'ah, "stripping away") is an intensive form (mubalaghah) of nazi', which is separating and cutting off.

(Al-shawa, "the limbs") is a collective noun of shawah, with a fatha on the shin and a light waw. It is the limb other than the head, such as the hand and the foot. So the plural is according to what each person has of limbs. It has also been said that shawah is the skin of the head, so the plural is in view of the number of people.

[Page 162]

And the clause ﴿تَدْعُو﴾ ("calls") is either a second predicate, according to the reading ﴿نَزَّاعَةٌ﴾ ("tearing away") in the nominative, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) according to both readings. The verb "calls" (*tad'ū*) may be used figuratively: the Fire is presented as a *metaphorical implicit* (*isti'āra makniyya*) comparison, in which the Fire is likened, in the crowding of people toward it, to a host inviting guests to a banquet. This is indicated by the word "calls," and it is in the manner of sarcasm (*tahakkum*).

The phrase ﴿مَنْ أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّى﴾ ("whoever turned his back and withdrew") and ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَى﴾ ("and gathered and hoarded") may serve as an indicator (*qarīna*) or as an abstraction (*tajrīd*), meaning: whoever turned his back and withdrew from faith in God. In it is antithesis (*ṭibāq*), because turning one's back and withdrawing are in general opposed to being called, since the normal state of one who is called is to come forward and not turn away. The verb ﴿تَدْعُو﴾ may be derived from *al-du'wa* with a *ḍamma* on the *dāl*. Alternatively, it may compare the summoning of the disbelievers to it with its calling them to attend, in the manner of a following comparison (*tab'iyya*), since the comparison is with the call of a caller. This is like the saying of Dhu al-Rumma describing a wild bull:

*amsā bi-Wahbayni mukhtāran limar'ihi ∗∗∗ min dhī al-Fawāris tad'ū anfahu al-Ribab*

He spent the night at Wahbayn, choosing it as his pasture, from Dhu al-Fawāris, while the *Ribab* call his nose.

*Al-Ribab*, with a *kasra* on the *rā'* and with two *bā'*s, is the plural of *ribba*, with a *kasra* on the *rā'* and a shadda on the *bā'*: a plant that grows green in summer.

It is also permissible that ﴿تَدْعُو﴾ be used literally, and that those who "call" are the angels appointed over Hell. The attribution of the calling to Hell is then a metaphorical attribution (*isnād majāzī*), either because it is the place of those who call, or because it is the cause of the calling. Or Hell itself calls literally, by God creating within it sounds that summon those who turned away to come to it, whereupon it devours them.

﴿مَنْ أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّى﴾ and ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَى﴾ denote the class of those described as having turned their backs, withdrawn, and gathered, and they are the criminals who wish that they could ransom themselves from the punishment of that day. These attributes are the distinguishing marks of the polytheists, and they are among the effects of the religion of polytheism, which is the strongest motive for their aversion from the call of Islam.

[Page 165]

These are three: turning one's back, withdrawing, and gathering wealth, that is, fear for their wealth.

*Al-Idbār* (turning one's back) is leaving something behind in the direction of the back, since *al-dubur* is the back. So *adbara* means he placed something behind him, either by not turning towards it at all, or by facing it and then departing from it.

*Al-Tawallī* is turning away from something and distancing oneself from it. Its origin is derived from *al-wilāya*, which is adherence (*al-mulāzama*). God said: ﴿فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ﴾ ("So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque") [al-Baqara 2:144]. Then they said *tawallā 'anhu* (he turned away from him), meaning he took another as a *walī* (protector), that is, he abandoned his guardianship for the guardianship of another, just as they said *raghiba fīhi* (he desired it) and *raghiba 'anhu* (he rejected it). Thus *tawallā* came to mean *adbara* and *a'rada* (turned away and withdrew). God said: ﴿عَنْ مَنْ تَوَلَّى عَنْ ذِكْرِنَا﴾ ("from him who turns away from Our remembrance") [al-Najm 53:29], that is, deal with him by turning away from him.

So in *tawallī* there is the meaning of preferring other than the one turned away from. For this reason there is a difference between *tawallī* and *idbār*, and by taking this difference into account, *wa-tawallā* is coordinated (*'uṭifa*) on *adbara*. The meaning is: it calls whoever has abandoned the truth and turned away from it to falsehood. This is a subtle point of the inimitability of the Qur'an (*i'jāz al-Qur'ān*): *idbār* may be intended as turning away without having turned, that is, turning away from the very first moment, while *tawallī* is intended as withdrawal after some engagement. For this reason, *idbār* is used metaphorically for not accepting the Qur'an and for refusing to listen to the call of the Messenger ﷺ, and this is the state of those about whom God said: ﴿وَقَالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَا تَسْمَعُوا لِهَذَا الْقُرْآنِ﴾ ("And those who disbelieve say: Do not listen to this Qur'an") [Fuṣṣilat 41:26]. And *tawallī* is used metaphorically for turning away from the Qur'an after hearing it, and for aversion from the call of the Messenger, as God said: ﴿وَإِذَا تُتْلَى عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتُنَا قَالُوا قَدْ سَمِعْنَا لَوْ نَشَاءُ لَقُلْنَا مِثْلَ هَذَا إِنْ هَذَا إِلَّا أَسَاطِيرُ الْأَوَّلِينَ﴾ ("And when Our verses are recited to them, they say: We have heard; if we wished, we could say the like of this. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients") [al-Anfāl 8:31]. Both states are states of disbelief and entail punishment, and both are combined in all the polytheists.

The purpose of mentioning them together is to denounce (*tafẓī'*) their possessors. On this view, the object of *adbara* and *tawallā* may be one shared object, governed by both verbs, and it may be supplied as something like "from the truth." In the *Kashshāf*: "he turned his back on the truth and withdrew from it," since what matters is the difference in the meanings of the two verbs, even if their object is one.

It is also permissible to supply for each verb an object that is more fitting to its meaning. Al-Bayḍāwī supplied: "he turned his back on the truth and withdrew from obedience," that is, he did not accept the truth, which is faith, from its root, and he withdrew from obedience to the Messenger after hearing his call. Qatāda gave the reverse: "he turned his back on obedience to God and withdrew from the Book of God." Al-Rāzī and al-Naysābūrī followed him.

[Page 166]

The gathering and hoarding in the phrase (﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَى﴾) are arranged so that the second follows the first. The ordering of the second after the first indicates that the omitted object of *jama'a* is something that is hoarded, that is, something placed in a container.

*Al-wi'ā'* is the container, that is, he gathered wealth and hoarded it and did not benefit the needy with it. From this comes the verb *awʿā* when someone is miserly. In the hadith: «ولا تُوعِي فَيُوعى عَلَيْكَ» ("Do not hoard, lest it be hoarded against you").

In the phrase *jama'a* there is an indication of greed (*ḥirṣ*), and in the phrase *fa-awʿā* there is an indication of long hope (*ṭūl al-amal*). From Qatāda: "(﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَى﴾) he was a gatherer of evil," and this is a good interpretation, namely, that an object is supplied for *jama'a* that the context indicates: that beyond his turning his back and withdrawing, he gathered evil qualities. In this case *fa-awʿā* is used metaphorically for his constant attachment to the evil qualities in him and his persistence in them, as though they were stored up and not to be let go.

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعًا﴾ ("Indeed, man was created anxious") ﴿إِذَا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعًا﴾ ("when evil touches him, he is distressed") ﴿وَإِذَا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعًا﴾ ("and when good touches him, he is withholding") are a parenthetical sentence (*mu'tariḍa*) between ﴿مَنْ أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّى﴾ ("whoever turned his back and withdrew"), ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَى﴾ ("and gathered and hoarded"), and the exception (*istithnā'*) "except those who pray," etc.

It is a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*) to the clause ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَى﴾, alerting to a disposition that lurks in human souls and moves them to greed in seeking what is beneficial, and to holding on to it for fear of its running out, because of the anxiety (*halaʿ*) within them. This is a concluding statement of reproach, and it is not in its context an excuse for one who gathered and hoarded, nor is it a reason for his action.

The placement of the emphatic particle (*ḥarf al-ta'kīd*) is due to what the sentence contains of wonder at this human disposition. So the emphasis serves merely to draw attention to the report, to call attention to it, and to hint at the need to beware of it.

The purpose of the concluding statement is His saying: (﴿وَإِذَا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعًا﴾). As for His saying (﴿إِذَا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعًا﴾), it is a preparation and a completion of his two states.

By *al-insān* is meant the species of man, not a specific individual, as in His saying: ﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ لَيَطْغَى﴾ ("Indeed, man transgresses") [al-'Alaq 96:6] ﴿أَنْ رَآهُ اسْتَغْنَى﴾ ("when he sees himself self-sufficient") [al-'Alaq 96:7], and His saying ﴿خُلِقَ الْإِنْسَانُ مِنْ عَجَلٍ﴾ ("Man was created of haste") [al-Anbiyā' 21:37]. Similar examples are numerous in the Qur'an.

[Page 167]

*Halū'* is an intensive form (*fa'ūl*, pattern of exaggeration) for being characterized by *al-halaʿ*.

*Al-Halaʿ* is an obscure word among the obscurities of the language, about which scholars have disputed. The *Kashshāf* says: "From Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, that is Thaʿlab, who said: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṭāhir said to me: What is *al-halaʿ*? I said: God has explained it, and there is no explanation clearer than His explanation, which is: the one who, when evil reaches him, shows extreme distress, and when good reaches him, he is stingy with it and withholds it from people." End. Thaʿlab's statement spread widely and satisfied many of the philologists from seeking further precision in defining *al-halaʿ*. Yet it is a statement not free from looseness and lack of precision of meaning. For if God's saying ﴿إِذَا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعًا﴾ ("when evil touches him, he is distressed") and ﴿وَإِذَا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعًا﴾ ("and when good touches him, he is withholding") is an explanation of the meaning of *jazūʿ*, then the word's meaning must be a compound of the meanings of the two clauses, so that the two clauses are an explanation of it. It is clear that the two meanings do not entail one another. Many of the masters of the language explained *al-halaʿ* as *al-jazaʿ*, or as intense *jazaʿ*, or as the most extreme *jazaʿ*. But *al-jazaʿ* is one of the effects of *al-halaʿ*, not its essence. For that does not hold in the saying of ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib:

*mā in jaziʿtu wa-lā halaʿtu ∗∗∗ wa-lā yaruddu bukāya zandā*

I have not been distressed, nor have I been anxious, and my weeping does not restore a spark (of fire, i.e., a dead man).

For he coordinates the negation of *halaʿ* with the negation of *jazaʿ*. If *halaʿ* were *jazaʿ*, the coordination would not be fitting; and if *halaʿ* were intense *jazaʿ*, the negation of it coordinated with the negation of *jazaʿ* would be superfluous (*ḥashw*). For this reason al-Marzūqī, in his commentary on the *Ḥamāsa*, strained greatly to explain the meaning of the verse, and it did not avail him anything. He said: "It is as if he said: I did not grieve over it with light, near grief, nor with severe, intense grief. This is a total negation of grief, like your saying: I did not see their small nor their great." End.

What I have deduced from tracing the uses of the word *halaʿ* is that *halaʿ* is the scarcity of self-restraint when something that grieves or gladdens the soul befalls, or when the expectation of that occurs and one is apprehensive about it. As for *jazaʿ*, it is among the effects of *halaʿ*. Some lexicographers explained *halaʿ* as greed (*sharah*), some as impatience (*ḍajar*), some as stinginess (*shuḥḥ*), some as hunger, and some as cowardice at the moment of encounter. What we have mentioned in defining it gathers these meanings together and shows you that they are effects of the attribute of *halaʿ*. The meaning of (﴿خُلِقَ هَلُوعًا﴾):

[Page 168]

*halaʿ* is an innate disposition within him together with his creation, which appears at the beginning of his awareness of what benefits and what harms him. So it is among his created dispositions, like the other human natures. For the construction of the circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) with its governing element does not indicate that the governing element is restricted to it, nor does the description of the one qualified by the state indicate that he has no attribute other than it. A thing may have a state and its opposite according to differing times and motives. By this, the prohibition of a state is coherent, even while its opposite is fully attainable by the one prohibited, because he must train his soul to resist deficiencies and remove them from himself. Since God mentioned *halaʿ* here right after the reproach of gathering and hoarding, it has indicated that man is able to restrain his *halaʿ* if he reflects on the consequences. Thus in His saying (﴿خُلِقَ هَلُوعًا﴾) there is a metonymy (*kināya*) through "creation" for the firm establishment of that disposition in him and its dominance over his soul.

The meaning is: it is part of the requirement of the composition of human perception that *halaʿ* arises within it.

The explanation of this is that the composition of the human faculties was established with a precise wisdom that makes them capable of acting and restraining, inclined to what is agreeable and turning away from what is repugnant. Within them were placed powers of opposite effects, and the intellect and perception manage their use as they should within the bounds of the bodily capacity given to the species and to each individual of the species. All of this is so that man may be fit for building up this earthly world, over which God made him a vicegerent (*khalīfa*), to reform it in a way that includes himself and those with him in this world, preparing him for his fitness to build up the world of eternity. Then He gave him a perception that distinguishes between the effects of existing things and the effects of their actions, between what benefits and what harms, and what has neither benefit nor harm. He created within him an inspiration that loves what benefits and hates what harms. Yet the mixing of the two qualities in some actions and some entities may show him their beneficial aspect and not their harmful aspect, so he seeks what he thinks is beneficial, without awareness of what harms lie hidden within it, in the immediate or the later term; or, aware of that, his eagerness for the immediate benefit makes him prefer taking it now, because he lacks the patience to forgo it, contriving excuses or stratagems through which he rushes into what harms him in the later term. The mixing of the inner faculties with the movements of thought may conceal from him the harm of the harmful and the benefit of the beneficial, so he does not find his way to what he should follow or avoid. Or it may not conceal this from him, but it creates in him a preference for following the harmful because of some agreeableness in it, even if for a time or at a passing moment, turning away from following the beneficial because of the burden in performing it or its repugnance to his feeling. This comes from the composition of his driving and restraining faculties and their instruments, through which they act and push, having some degree of reversal in their operations. From this marvellous composition arose a capacity for fulfilling the good management entrusted to man, and also a capacity for corrupting that or scattering it.

[Page 169]

However, God gave man intellect and wisdom, which, if he uses them well, purify his character and straighten his crookedness. He did not leave him without callers to good who describe to him how to train his unruly soul, and how to reconcile his perception with his sensation. These are the Messengers, the Prophets, and the wise.

When the human being is described as being deeply afflicted with certain deficiencies, and this is framed as though he was created with them, the purpose is to place the responsibility for them upon him, because he neglected to train his soul in what it contains of the disposition toward good, and he gave it free rein to reach the furthest extent of evil, and he neglected the counsel of the revealed laws and of the wise.

When what the human being attains of good is attributed to God Most High, the purpose is to draw attention to God's blessing upon him in creating within him the capacity that brings about good, and the blessing of His guidance and of awakening him to the truth. This is indicated by the words of God Most High: ﴿Whatever good befalls you, it is from God, and whatever evil befalls you, it is from yourself﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:79), following His words: ﴿Say, "All of it is from God." So what is wrong with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:78). In this domain, the understandings of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) slipped, the horizons grew dark for them, so they reflected and calculated, yet they found no way out and could not manage it.

Know that the expression (khuliqa al-insanu, "the human being was created"), when it is connected to something that is not a material substance, as in ﴿Indeed, We created the human being from a drop of mixed fluid﴾ (al-Insan 76:2), but rather to something of character traits and innate dispositions, may be intended to draw attention to the innate nature of the human being, and that it hastens to become attached to his inclinations when he acts, thereby alluding to the necessity of guarding against its dangers, as in ﴿The human being was created of haste﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:37), and ﴿Indeed, the human being was created anxious﴾ (al-Ma'arij 70:19). It may also occur for the sake of excusing and gentleness, as in His words: ﴿God wishes to lighten for you, and the human being was created weak﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:28). It may also occur to explain the origin of what the human being was made upon and what has come upon him of bad conduct in his actions, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿We certainly created the human being in the best of stature, then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ (al-Tin 95:4). Thus the verb "created" in such cases is used figuratively, on account of the great extent of association.

ʿUrwah ibn Udhaynah said:

*Indeed, she who claimed that she had grown weary of your heart, *
*Was created as your love, just as you were created as her love.*

He intended to refute the idea that she grew weary of him, on the grounds that she was created as his beloved just as his beloved was created for him; that is, his love for her does not separate from him.

Al-halaʿ (anxiety, impatience) is a blameworthy quality, so describing the human being with it here is a reproach against him for falling short in adopting the character of repelling its effects. For this reason, the phrase ﴿and he gathered and hoarded﴾ is appended to it, in accordance with both of its meanings.

The word (jazūʿan, "prone to panic") is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl) referring to the concealed pronoun in (halūʿan), or as a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl), because the state of halaʿ includes panic upon being touched by evil.

His words (manūʿan, "prone to withholding") are coordinated with (jazūʿan), meaning: he was created anxious, in a state in which he is prone to panic when evil touches him, and prone to withholding when good touches him.

Al-sharr (evil) is harm, such as sickness and poverty. Al-khayr (good) is what benefits the human being and suits his desires, such as health and wealth. Al-jazūʿ is one who panics intensely, and al-jaza' is the opposite of patience. Al-manūʿ is one who withholds much, that is, one who is intensely stingy in giving away anything of the good that he possesses.

The (idhā, "when") in both places are two adverbial clauses, each of which is connected to the description it is attached to, namely (jazūʿan) and (manūʿan).

Page 170

[Page 159]

It is permissible for ﴿on the day the sky will be﴾ to be linked to the verb (ta'ruju, "ascend") [in the preceding verse], and it is also permissible for it to be linked to (yawaddu al-mujrimu, "the guilty one would wish"), being placed before it for emphasis on mentioning the day. In that case, His saying ﴿on the day the sky will be like molten metal﴾ is the beginning of a new statement. A sentence that is made the beginning of a statement is treated as a comprehensive substitute (badal al-ishtimal, a substitute that encompasses what precedes it) for the sentence ﴿and no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend﴾, because the absence of questioning is caused by the severity of the terror, and among what that terror encompasses is that the one who turns away would wish to ransom himself from that punishment.

Al-muhl (molten metal) means the dregs of oil. The meaning is the comparison of the sky, in the dissolving of its parts, to oil. This is like His saying in Surat al-Rahman ﴿and it became red like tanned leather﴾ [al-Rahman: 37].

Al-ihn (wool) means dyed wool. It has been said that it means dyed in general, and it has been said that it means dyed in various colours, and this is the view adopted by al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) and al-Zamakhshari. Zuhayr said:

"The crumbs of dyed wool in every abode they alighted at were like the seeds of the al-Fana plant, unbroken."

Al-Fana, with a short alif, is a seed in the desert, called ʿinab al-thaʿlab (fox grapes), and it has colours: some of it is green, some yellow, and some red. Al-ʿihnah is a tree in the desert that has red blossoms.

The point of resemblance with wool is the scattering of the parts, as it came in the verse of al-Qari'ah ﴿and the mountains will be like carded wool﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 5]. The singling out of wool for mention is to complete the resemblance, because the mountains have colours. He, exalted is He, said ﴿and among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of varying colours﴾ [Fatir: 27]. The sky and the mountains will be in this state only when the cohesion of their parts is dissolved at the passing away of this world and the transition to the world of the Hereafter.

The meaning of ﴿and no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend﴾ is that, because of the severity of the terror that befalls people, one who sees his intimate friend in distress and hardship will not have leisure to ask him about his condition, because he is occupied with something else. Thus the object of (yas'alu, "asks") is omitted, as it is evident from the context and from His saying (yubassarunahum, "they will be shown to them"). That is, intimate friends will see the states of their intimate friends in distress, so no intimate friend will ask after another. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

[Page 160]

"Every intimate friend I had hoped for said: 'I will not distract you, for I am busy with myself regarding you.'"

Al-hamim means the close friend, the companion.

Al-Jumhur read (yas'alu) with a fatha on the ya', in the active voice. Abu Ja'far and al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, read it with a damma on the ya', in the passive voice. Then the meaning is: no intimate friend will be asked about an intimate friend, with the preposition omitted.

The position of (yubassarunahum, "they will be shown to them") is an explanatory resumptive clause (al-istinaf al-bayani, a new sentence answering an implied question) to dispel the possibility that it might occur to the listener that close friends do not see one another that day, because everyone is occupied. So it is answered that they will be shown their close ones, so that they see what they are suffering of punishment, and so they will be given punishment upon punishment.

It is also permissible for the clause (yubassarunahum) to be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). That is, no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend while every intimate friend sees his intimate friend, and it is said to him: "Look at what so-and-so is suffering."

(Yubassarunahum) is the present tense of basarahu bi-l-amr, meaning he made him see it, that is, made him a viewer of it. Its origin is yubassaruna bihim, so the preposition was dropped and the verb was made to take a direct object.

The two pronouns refer to (hamimun, "intimate friend") in the nominative and to (hamiman, "intimate friend") in the accusative. That is, every intimate friend sees his intimate friend. The two pronouns are plural, in view of the generality of (hamimun) and (hamiman) in a negative context.

(Yawaddu) means he loves, that is, he wishes. This may happen through a thought that comes to his mind on seeing the punishment, or through a statement that issues from him, like His saying ﴿and the disbeliever will say: "Would that I were dust!"﴾ [al-Naba': 40]. This is the apparent meaning, that is, the disbeliever will cry out on that day and say: "I would ransom myself from the punishment with my sons, my spouse and my kin," and this will be a disgrace for him that day before his family.

Al-mujrim is one who commits a jurm, which is a great sin, namely disbelief, because at the beginning of the mission people were of two kinds: disbelievers and obedient believers.

(Yawma'idhin, "that day") is the same as ﴿the day the sky will be like molten metal﴾. If His saying ﴿the day the sky will be﴾ is linked to (yawaddu), then His saying (yawma'idhin) is an emphasis of ﴿the day the sky will be like molten metal﴾. If it is linked to His saying (ta'ruju al-malaikatu, "the angels ascend"), then His saying (yawma'idhin) conveys that this day is the day when the guilty one would wish to ransom himself from punishment with those mentioned after it.

[Page 161]

(Law, "would that") is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), so what follows it is in the position of the object of (yawaddu), that is: the day of ransoming oneself from punishment with his sons, and so on to the end of the verse.

Al-Jumhur read (yawmi'idhin) with a kasra on the mim of (yawm), in the genitive, by the annexation of (adhab, "punishment") to it. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha on the mim, as its being built on the annexation of (yawm) to (idh), which is an indeclinable noun. Both readings are permissible.

Al-iftida' means giving a ransom (fida'), which is what is given as a substitute for rescue from a consequence. From it is His saying ﴿and if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85] in al-Baqarah, and His saying ﴿even if he were to ransom himself with it﴾ in Al 'Imran. The meaning is: would that he ransom himself. The preposition (bi-) after the root of ransom introduces the substitute given, so the meaning of (bi-) is substitution.

The meaning of (min, "from") is figurative origin, since the verb (yaftadi, "ransoms himself") is taken to mean (yatakhallasu, "frees himself"). (Sahibatuhu, "his spouse") means his wife.

Al-fasilah (kin) means the nearest relatives of the tribe, and they are the relatives who are separated from one, that is, those who are extracted from one. So it includes fathers and mothers. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Ashhab said: "I asked Malik about the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿and his kin who shelters him﴾, and he said: 'It is his mother.'" Meaning: the father is understood from it by the way of implication (lahn al-khitab, what is understood from the implied sense of the speech). So the nearest kin are fully mentioned, both explicitly and by implication. As for the well-known interpretation, al-fasilah indicates the fathers by the wording, and the mothers are derived by the implication of the discourse.

The relatives have been arranged according to the degree of natural inclination towards them in common custom, because natural inclination arises from constant companionship and frequent association.

He did not mention the two parents, because they are included in al-fasilah, for the sake of brevity.

Al-iwa' means gathering together and taking refuge. He, exalted is He, said ﴿he took his brother to himself﴾ [Yusuf: 69], and He said ﴿I will take refuge in a mountain﴾ [Hud: 43].

As for (allati tu'wihi, "who shelters him"): if it means the tribe, then al-iwa' is a figurative usage for protection and support, that is, and despite that he would ransom himself with them, knowing that they will not avail him anything that day. If it means the mother, then al-iwa' is in its literal sense, with regard to the past tense and the present-tense form, to bring the state vividly before the mind, like His saying ﴿and Allah is He who sends the winds, so they raise clouds﴾ [Fatir: 9]. That is: he would wish to ransom himself with his mother, despite the strength of his attachment to her, since she used to shelter him. So the choice of the word (fasilatihi, "his kin") and the verb (tu'wihi, "shelters him") here is part of the concision and inimitability of the Qur'an, to include all these meanings.

([wa-man fi al-ardi jami'an, "and all who are on earth"]) is coordinated with (banihi, "his sons"), that is: and he would ransom himself with whoever is on earth, that is, whoever belongs to him on earth of what is dear to him, such as intimate friends, relatives, and precious wealth, which people are usually stingy about giving and eager to keep, in the manner of His saying ﴿so there will not be accepted from any of them the earth full of gold, even if he ransomed himself with it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91].

The relative pronoun (man) is used to give precedence to the rational over the non-rational, because among them are intimate friends.

(Thumma, "then") in His saying (thumma yunjihi, "then it would save him") indicates a sequence of rank, that is: he would wish to give all that and to be saved from the punishment by the ransom. So being saved from punishment is the most important thing for the guilty one in his longing. The prominent pronoun in His saying (yunjihi) refers to the ransoming that is understood from (yaftadi, "ransoms himself"), in the manner of His saying ﴿be just, that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8].

The clause coordinated with (thumma) is the consequence of the longing, so the apparent expectation was that it would be coordinated with (fa, "so"), which is the more common usage in such cases, as in His saying ﴿they wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike﴾ [al-Nisa': 89], and His saying ﴿they wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam: 9]. But here He changed from coordinating with (fa) to coordinating with (thumma), to indicate the intensity of the guilty one's concern for salvation by any means.

The object of (yunjihi) is omitted, and it is indicated by His saying (min 'adhabi yawma'idhin, "from the punishment of that day").

(Kalla, "No!") is a particle of repulsion and nullification of a preceding statement, and it is not free of having a statement mentioned after it. Here it serves to nullify what the longing of the guilty one entertains in his soul, and it takes the place of a statement, because Allah is aware of it, or to nullify what is uttered of wishing for that. He, exalted is He, said ﴿and the disbeliever will say: "Would that I were dust!"﴾ [al-Naba': 40]. Do you not see that He expressed that statement by the longing in His saying ﴿that day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth would be levelled over them﴾ [al-Nisa': 42], that is, that they would become part of its dust.

So the implied meaning is: it is said to him, "No!" That is: no ransoming and no salvation.

The sentence (﴿indeed it is a blazing fire﴾) is an explanatory resumptive clause, arising from what the particle (kalla, "No!") conveys of nullification. The pronoun of (innaha, "indeed it") refers to what the guilty one sees before him of the sight of Hell. So He informed that this is a blazing fire (la?a). Since (la?a) is accompanied by the feminine alif, the pronoun is made feminine in accordance with the feminine gender of the predicate, and its subject is followed by descriptive attributes. The purpose is an indirect allusion that it has been prepared for him, that is: it will burn you and strip away your limbs. And what the indirect allusion pointed to is stated explicitly in His saying ﴿calling him who turned his back and withdrew, and gathered and hoarded﴾, that is: it calls you, O one who turned his back on the call to monotheism and withdrew from it and was concerned only with gathering wealth.

So the particle (inna, "indeed") is for emphasis of the indirect allusive meaning of the statement, not for the report that what he sees is a blazing fire, since that is not a matter open to doubt. (La?a) is the predicate of (inna).

It is also permissible for the pronoun of (innaha) to be the pronoun of the matter (dhamir al-qissah, the pronoun of the situation or affair), that is: indeed your situation and affair is a blazing fire. Then (la?a) would be the subject.

Al-Jumhur read (nazza'atun, "stripping away") in the nominative, so it is a second predicate of (inna) if the pronoun is taken to refer to the fire that is seen, or it is a predicate of (la?a) if the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter and (la?a) is taken as the subject.

Hafs read it in the accusative as a circumstantial state, so according to Hafs's reading it is necessary that the pronoun is not the pronoun of the matter. The indirect allusion is the same, and the particle (inna) is either for emphasis directed at the allusive meaning, as already explained, or merely for giving special importance to the sentence that follows it, because sentences opening with the pronoun of the matter are among the statements given special importance.

(La?a) is a proper noun transferred from the noun meaning "blaze", and it was made a proper noun for (jahannam, "Hell"). Its alif is the alif of feminine gender. Its original form was la?an, on the pattern of fatan, with tanwin, as a common noun for the blaze of fire. The common noun was transferred to become a proper noun for one specific member of its kind, and so it was given the feminine alif, as an indication, by that change, of its transfer to the status of a proper noun.

The Arabs sometimes introduce a change to a word that is not a proper noun when they transfer it to the status of a proper noun, as they named Shams with a damma on the shin, transferred from Shams with a fatha on the shin, as Ibn Jinni said in explaining the verse of Ta'abbata Sharran:

"Indeed I am one who sends forth my praise, aiming it at the son of the uncle of truth, Shums ibn Malik."

It is not a proper noun by dominance, since it is neither definite nor annexed. Because it combines being a proper noun and being feminine, it is prohibited from taking tanwin. So you do not say la?an with tanwin unless you mean the common kind of blaze, and you do not say al-la?a unless you mean a particular blaze. But if you mean the name of Hell, you say la?a with the feminine alif, without tanwin and without the definite article.

(Nazza'ah, "stripping away") is an intensive form (mubalaghah) of nazi', which is separating and cutting off.

(Al-shawa, "the limbs") is a collective noun of shawah, with a fatha on the shin and a light waw. It is the limb other than the head, such as the hand and the foot. So the plural is according to what each person has of limbs. It has also been said that shawah is the skin of the head, so the plural is in view of the number of people.

[Page 162]

And the clause ﴿تَدْعُو﴾ ("calls") is either a second predicate, according to the reading ﴿نَزَّاعَةٌ﴾ ("tearing away") in the nominative, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) according to both readings. The verb "calls" (*tad'ū*) may be used figuratively: the Fire is presented as a *metaphorical implicit* (*isti'āra makniyya*) comparison, in which the Fire is likened, in the crowding of people toward it, to a host inviting guests to a banquet. This is indicated by the word "calls," and it is in the manner of sarcasm (*tahakkum*).

The phrase ﴿مَنْ أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّى﴾ ("whoever turned his back and withdrew") and ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَى﴾ ("and gathered and hoarded") may serve as an indicator (*qarīna*) or as an abstraction (*tajrīd*), meaning: whoever turned his back and withdrew from faith in God. In it is antithesis (*ṭibāq*), because turning one's back and withdrawing are in general opposed to being called, since the normal state of one who is called is to come forward and not turn away. The verb ﴿تَدْعُو﴾ may be derived from *al-du'wa* with a *ḍamma* on the *dāl*. Alternatively, it may compare the summoning of the disbelievers to it with its calling them to attend, in the manner of a following comparison (*tab'iyya*), since the comparison is with the call of a caller. This is like the saying of Dhu al-Rumma describing a wild bull:

*amsā bi-Wahbayni mukhtāran limar'ihi ∗∗∗ min dhī al-Fawāris tad'ū anfahu al-Ribab*

He spent the night at Wahbayn, choosing it as his pasture, from Dhu al-Fawāris, while the *Ribab* call his nose.

*Al-Ribab*, with a *kasra* on the *rā'* and with two *bā'*s, is the plural of *ribba*, with a *kasra* on the *rā'* and a shadda on the *bā'*: a plant that grows green in summer.

It is also permissible that ﴿تَدْعُو﴾ be used literally, and that those who "call" are the angels appointed over Hell. The attribution of the calling to Hell is then a metaphorical attribution (*isnād majāzī*), either because it is the place of those who call, or because it is the cause of the calling. Or Hell itself calls literally, by God creating within it sounds that summon those who turned away to come to it, whereupon it devours them.

﴿مَنْ أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّى﴾ and ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَى﴾ denote the class of those described as having turned their backs, withdrawn, and gathered, and they are the criminals who wish that they could ransom themselves from the punishment of that day. These attributes are the distinguishing marks of the polytheists, and they are among the effects of the religion of polytheism, which is the strongest motive for their aversion from the call of Islam.

[Page 165]

These are three: turning one's back, withdrawing, and gathering wealth, that is, fear for their wealth.

*Al-Idbār* (turning one's back) is leaving something behind in the direction of the back, since *al-dubur* is the back. So *adbara* means he placed something behind him, either by not turning towards it at all, or by facing it and then departing from it.

*Al-Tawallī* is turning away from something and distancing oneself from it. Its origin is derived from *al-wilāya*, which is adherence (*al-mulāzama*). God said: ﴿فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ﴾ ("So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque") [al-Baqara 2:144]. Then they said *tawallā 'anhu* (he turned away from him), meaning he took another as a *walī* (protector), that is, he abandoned his guardianship for the guardianship of another, just as they said *raghiba fīhi* (he desired it) and *raghiba 'anhu* (he rejected it). Thus *tawallā* came to mean *adbara* and *a'rada* (turned away and withdrew). God said: ﴿عَنْ مَنْ تَوَلَّى عَنْ ذِكْرِنَا﴾ ("from him who turns away from Our remembrance") [al-Najm 53:29], that is, deal with him by turning away from him.

So in *tawallī* there is the meaning of preferring other than the one turned away from. For this reason there is a difference between *tawallī* and *idbār*, and by taking this difference into account, *wa-tawallā* is coordinated (*'uṭifa*) on *adbara*. The meaning is: it calls whoever has abandoned the truth and turned away from it to falsehood. This is a subtle point of the inimitability of the Qur'an (*i'jāz al-Qur'ān*): *idbār* may be intended as turning away without having turned, that is, turning away from the very first moment, while *tawallī* is intended as withdrawal after some engagement. For this reason, *idbār* is used metaphorically for not accepting the Qur'an and for refusing to listen to the call of the Messenger ﷺ, and this is the state of those about whom God said: ﴿وَقَالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَا تَسْمَعُوا لِهَذَا الْقُرْآنِ﴾ ("And those who disbelieve say: Do not listen to this Qur'an") [Fuṣṣilat 41:26]. And *tawallī* is used metaphorically for turning away from the Qur'an after hearing it, and for aversion from the call of the Messenger, as God said: ﴿وَإِذَا تُتْلَى عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتُنَا قَالُوا قَدْ سَمِعْنَا لَوْ نَشَاءُ لَقُلْنَا مِثْلَ هَذَا إِنْ هَذَا إِلَّا أَسَاطِيرُ الْأَوَّلِينَ﴾ ("And when Our verses are recited to them, they say: We have heard; if we wished, we could say the like of this. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients") [al-Anfāl 8:31]. Both states are states of disbelief and entail punishment, and both are combined in all the polytheists.

The purpose of mentioning them together is to denounce (*tafẓī'*) their possessors. On this view, the object of *adbara* and *tawallā* may be one shared object, governed by both verbs, and it may be supplied as something like "from the truth." In the *Kashshāf*: "he turned his back on the truth and withdrew from it," since what matters is the difference in the meanings of the two verbs, even if their object is one.

It is also permissible to supply for each verb an object that is more fitting to its meaning. Al-Bayḍāwī supplied: "he turned his back on the truth and withdrew from obedience," that is, he did not accept the truth, which is faith, from its root, and he withdrew from obedience to the Messenger after hearing his call. Qatāda gave the reverse: "he turned his back on obedience to God and withdrew from the Book of God." Al-Rāzī and al-Naysābūrī followed him.

[Page 166]

The gathering and hoarding in the phrase (﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَى﴾) are arranged so that the second follows the first. The ordering of the second after the first indicates that the omitted object of *jama'a* is something that is hoarded, that is, something placed in a container.

*Al-wi'ā'* is the container, that is, he gathered wealth and hoarded it and did not benefit the needy with it. From this comes the verb *awʿā* when someone is miserly. In the hadith: «ولا تُوعِي فَيُوعى عَلَيْكَ» ("Do not hoard, lest it be hoarded against you").

In the phrase *jama'a* there is an indication of greed (*ḥirṣ*), and in the phrase *fa-awʿā* there is an indication of long hope (*ṭūl al-amal*). From Qatāda: "(﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَى﴾) he was a gatherer of evil," and this is a good interpretation, namely, that an object is supplied for *jama'a* that the context indicates: that beyond his turning his back and withdrawing, he gathered evil qualities. In this case *fa-awʿā* is used metaphorically for his constant attachment to the evil qualities in him and his persistence in them, as though they were stored up and not to be let go.

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعًا﴾ ("Indeed, man was created anxious") ﴿إِذَا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعًا﴾ ("when evil touches him, he is distressed") ﴿وَإِذَا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعًا﴾ ("and when good touches him, he is withholding") are a parenthetical sentence (*mu'tariḍa*) between ﴿مَنْ أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّى﴾ ("whoever turned his back and withdrew"), ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَى﴾ ("and gathered and hoarded"), and the exception (*istithnā'*) "except those who pray," etc.

It is a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*) to the clause ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَى﴾, alerting to a disposition that lurks in human souls and moves them to greed in seeking what is beneficial, and to holding on to it for fear of its running out, because of the anxiety (*halaʿ*) within them. This is a concluding statement of reproach, and it is not in its context an excuse for one who gathered and hoarded, nor is it a reason for his action.

The placement of the emphatic particle (*ḥarf al-ta'kīd*) is due to what the sentence contains of wonder at this human disposition. So the emphasis serves merely to draw attention to the report, to call attention to it, and to hint at the need to beware of it.

The purpose of the concluding statement is His saying: (﴿وَإِذَا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعًا﴾). As for His saying (﴿إِذَا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعًا﴾), it is a preparation and a completion of his two states.

By *al-insān* is meant the species of man, not a specific individual, as in His saying: ﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ لَيَطْغَى﴾ ("Indeed, man transgresses") [al-'Alaq 96:6] ﴿أَنْ رَآهُ اسْتَغْنَى﴾ ("when he sees himself self-sufficient") [al-'Alaq 96:7], and His saying ﴿خُلِقَ الْإِنْسَانُ مِنْ عَجَلٍ﴾ ("Man was created of haste") [al-Anbiyā' 21:37]. Similar examples are numerous in the Qur'an.

[Page 167]

*Halū'* is an intensive form (*fa'ūl*, pattern of exaggeration) for being characterized by *al-halaʿ*.

*Al-Halaʿ* is an obscure word among the obscurities of the language, about which scholars have disputed. The *Kashshāf* says: "From Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, that is Thaʿlab, who said: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṭāhir said to me: What is *al-halaʿ*? I said: God has explained it, and there is no explanation clearer than His explanation, which is: the one who, when evil reaches him, shows extreme distress, and when good reaches him, he is stingy with it and withholds it from people." End. Thaʿlab's statement spread widely and satisfied many of the philologists from seeking further precision in defining *al-halaʿ*. Yet it is a statement not free from looseness and lack of precision of meaning. For if God's saying ﴿إِذَا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعًا﴾ ("when evil touches him, he is distressed") and ﴿وَإِذَا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعًا﴾ ("and when good touches him, he is withholding") is an explanation of the meaning of *jazūʿ*, then the word's meaning must be a compound of the meanings of the two clauses, so that the two clauses are an explanation of it. It is clear that the two meanings do not entail one another. Many of the masters of the language explained *al-halaʿ* as *al-jazaʿ*, or as intense *jazaʿ*, or as the most extreme *jazaʿ*. But *al-jazaʿ* is one of the effects of *al-halaʿ*, not its essence. For that does not hold in the saying of ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib:

*mā in jaziʿtu wa-lā halaʿtu ∗∗∗ wa-lā yaruddu bukāya zandā*

I have not been distressed, nor have I been anxious, and my weeping does not restore a spark (of fire, i.e., a dead man).

For he coordinates the negation of *halaʿ* with the negation of *jazaʿ*. If *halaʿ* were *jazaʿ*, the coordination would not be fitting; and if *halaʿ* were intense *jazaʿ*, the negation of it coordinated with the negation of *jazaʿ* would be superfluous (*ḥashw*). For this reason al-Marzūqī, in his commentary on the *Ḥamāsa*, strained greatly to explain the meaning of the verse, and it did not avail him anything. He said: "It is as if he said: I did not grieve over it with light, near grief, nor with severe, intense grief. This is a total negation of grief, like your saying: I did not see their small nor their great." End.

What I have deduced from tracing the uses of the word *halaʿ* is that *halaʿ* is the scarcity of self-restraint when something that grieves or gladdens the soul befalls, or when the expectation of that occurs and one is apprehensive about it. As for *jazaʿ*, it is among the effects of *halaʿ*. Some lexicographers explained *halaʿ* as greed (*sharah*), some as impatience (*ḍajar*), some as stinginess (*shuḥḥ*), some as hunger, and some as cowardice at the moment of encounter. What we have mentioned in defining it gathers these meanings together and shows you that they are effects of the attribute of *halaʿ*. The meaning of (﴿خُلِقَ هَلُوعًا﴾):

[Page 168]

*halaʿ* is an innate disposition within him together with his creation, which appears at the beginning of his awareness of what benefits and what harms him. So it is among his created dispositions, like the other human natures. For the construction of the circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) with its governing element does not indicate that the governing element is restricted to it, nor does the description of the one qualified by the state indicate that he has no attribute other than it. A thing may have a state and its opposite according to differing times and motives. By this, the prohibition of a state is coherent, even while its opposite is fully attainable by the one prohibited, because he must train his soul to resist deficiencies and remove them from himself. Since God mentioned *halaʿ* here right after the reproach of gathering and hoarding, it has indicated that man is able to restrain his *halaʿ* if he reflects on the consequences. Thus in His saying (﴿خُلِقَ هَلُوعًا﴾) there is a metonymy (*kināya*) through "creation" for the firm establishment of that disposition in him and its dominance over his soul.

The meaning is: it is part of the requirement of the composition of human perception that *halaʿ* arises within it.

The explanation of this is that the composition of the human faculties was established with a precise wisdom that makes them capable of acting and restraining, inclined to what is agreeable and turning away from what is repugnant. Within them were placed powers of opposite effects, and the intellect and perception manage their use as they should within the bounds of the bodily capacity given to the species and to each individual of the species. All of this is so that man may be fit for building up this earthly world, over which God made him a vicegerent (*khalīfa*), to reform it in a way that includes himself and those with him in this world, preparing him for his fitness to build up the world of eternity. Then He gave him a perception that distinguishes between the effects of existing things and the effects of their actions, between what benefits and what harms, and what has neither benefit nor harm. He created within him an inspiration that loves what benefits and hates what harms. Yet the mixing of the two qualities in some actions and some entities may show him their beneficial aspect and not their harmful aspect, so he seeks what he thinks is beneficial, without awareness of what harms lie hidden within it, in the immediate or the later term; or, aware of that, his eagerness for the immediate benefit makes him prefer taking it now, because he lacks the patience to forgo it, contriving excuses or stratagems through which he rushes into what harms him in the later term. The mixing of the inner faculties with the movements of thought may conceal from him the harm of the harmful and the benefit of the beneficial, so he does not find his way to what he should follow or avoid. Or it may not conceal this from him, but it creates in him a preference for following the harmful because of some agreeableness in it, even if for a time or at a passing moment, turning away from following the beneficial because of the burden in performing it or its repugnance to his feeling. This comes from the composition of his driving and restraining faculties and their instruments, through which they act and push, having some degree of reversal in their operations. From this marvellous composition arose a capacity for fulfilling the good management entrusted to man, and also a capacity for corrupting that or scattering it.

[Page 169]

However, God gave man intellect and wisdom, which, if he uses them well, purify his character and straighten his crookedness. He did not leave him without callers to good who describe to him how to train his unruly soul, and how to reconcile his perception with his sensation. These are the Messengers, the Prophets, and the wise.

When the human being is described as being deeply afflicted with certain deficiencies, and this is framed as though he was created with them, the purpose is to place the responsibility for them upon him, because he neglected to train his soul in what it contains of the disposition toward good, and he gave it free rein to reach the furthest extent of evil, and he neglected the counsel of the revealed laws and of the wise.

When what the human being attains of good is attributed to God Most High, the purpose is to draw attention to God's blessing upon him in creating within him the capacity that brings about good, and the blessing of His guidance and of awakening him to the truth. This is indicated by the words of God Most High: ﴿Whatever good befalls you, it is from God, and whatever evil befalls you, it is from yourself﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:79), following His words: ﴿Say, "All of it is from God." So what is wrong with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:78). In this domain, the understandings of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) slipped, the horizons grew dark for them, so they reflected and calculated, yet they found no way out and could not manage it.

Know that the expression (khuliqa al-insanu, "the human being was created"), when it is connected to something that is not a material substance, as in ﴿Indeed, We created the human being from a drop of mixed fluid﴾ (al-Insan 76:2), but rather to something of character traits and innate dispositions, may be intended to draw attention to the innate nature of the human being, and that it hastens to become attached to his inclinations when he acts, thereby alluding to the necessity of guarding against its dangers, as in ﴿The human being was created of haste﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:37), and ﴿Indeed, the human being was created anxious﴾ (al-Ma'arij 70:19). It may also occur for the sake of excusing and gentleness, as in His words: ﴿God wishes to lighten for you, and the human being was created weak﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:28). It may also occur to explain the origin of what the human being was made upon and what has come upon him of bad conduct in his actions, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿We certainly created the human being in the best of stature, then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ (al-Tin 95:4). Thus the verb "created" in such cases is used figuratively, on account of the great extent of association.

ʿUrwah ibn Udhaynah said:

*Indeed, she who claimed that she had grown weary of your heart, *
*Was created as your love, just as you were created as her love.*

He intended to refute the idea that she grew weary of him, on the grounds that she was created as his beloved just as his beloved was created for him; that is, his love for her does not separate from him.

Al-halaʿ (anxiety, impatience) is a blameworthy quality, so describing the human being with it here is a reproach against him for falling short in adopting the character of repelling its effects. For this reason, the phrase ﴿and he gathered and hoarded﴾ is appended to it, in accordance with both of its meanings.

The word (jazūʿan, "prone to panic") is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl) referring to the concealed pronoun in (halūʿan), or as a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl), because the state of halaʿ includes panic upon being touched by evil.

His words (manūʿan, "prone to withholding") are coordinated with (jazūʿan), meaning: he was created anxious, in a state in which he is prone to panic when evil touches him, and prone to withholding when good touches him.

Al-sharr (evil) is harm, such as sickness and poverty. Al-khayr (good) is what benefits the human being and suits his desires, such as health and wealth. Al-jazūʿ is one who panics intensely, and al-jaza' is the opposite of patience. Al-manūʿ is one who withholds much, that is, one who is intensely stingy in giving away anything of the good that he possesses.

The (idhā, "when") in both places are two adverbial clauses, each of which is connected to the description it is attached to, namely (jazūʿan) and (manūʿan).

Page 170

[Page 159]

It is permissible for ﴿on the day the sky will be﴾ to be linked to the verb (ta'ruju, "ascend") [in the preceding verse], and it is also permissible for it to be linked to (yawaddu al-mujrimu, "the guilty one would wish"), being placed before it for emphasis on mentioning the day. In that case, His saying ﴿on the day the sky will be like molten metal﴾ is the beginning of a new statement. A sentence that is made the beginning of a statement is treated as a comprehensive substitute (badal al-ishtimal, a substitute that encompasses what precedes it) for the sentence ﴿and no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend﴾, because the absence of questioning is caused by the severity of the terror, and among what that terror encompasses is that the one who turns away would wish to ransom himself from that punishment.

Al-muhl (molten metal) means the dregs of oil. The meaning is the comparison of the sky, in the dissolving of its parts, to oil. This is like His saying in Surat al-Rahman ﴿and it became red like tanned leather﴾ [al-Rahman: 37].

Al-ihn (wool) means dyed wool. It has been said that it means dyed in general, and it has been said that it means dyed in various colours, and this is the view adopted by al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) and al-Zamakhshari. Zuhayr said:

"The crumbs of dyed wool in every abode they alighted at were like the seeds of the al-Fana plant, unbroken."

Al-Fana, with a short alif, is a seed in the desert, called ʿinab al-thaʿlab (fox grapes), and it has colours: some of it is green, some yellow, and some red. Al-ʿihnah is a tree in the desert that has red blossoms.

The point of resemblance with wool is the scattering of the parts, as it came in the verse of al-Qari'ah ﴿and the mountains will be like carded wool﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 5]. The singling out of wool for mention is to complete the resemblance, because the mountains have colours. He, exalted is He, said ﴿and among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of varying colours﴾ [Fatir: 27]. The sky and the mountains will be in this state only when the cohesion of their parts is dissolved at the passing away of this world and the transition to the world of the Hereafter.

The meaning of ﴿and no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend﴾ is that, because of the severity of the terror that befalls people, one who sees his intimate friend in distress and hardship will not have leisure to ask him about his condition, because he is occupied with something else. Thus the object of (yas'alu, "asks") is omitted, as it is evident from the context and from His saying (yubassarunahum, "they will be shown to them"). That is, intimate friends will see the states of their intimate friends in distress, so no intimate friend will ask after another. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

[Page 160]

"Every intimate friend I had hoped for said: 'I will not distract you, for I am busy with myself regarding you.'"

Al-hamim means the close friend, the companion.

Al-Jumhur read (yas'alu) with a fatha on the ya', in the active voice. Abu Ja'far and al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, read it with a damma on the ya', in the passive voice. Then the meaning is: no intimate friend will be asked about an intimate friend, with the preposition omitted.

The position of (yubassarunahum, "they will be shown to them") is an explanatory resumptive clause (al-istinaf al-bayani, a new sentence answering an implied question) to dispel the possibility that it might occur to the listener that close friends do not see one another that day, because everyone is occupied. So it is answered that they will be shown their close ones, so that they see what they are suffering of punishment, and so they will be given punishment upon punishment.

It is also permissible for the clause (yubassarunahum) to be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). That is, no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend while every intimate friend sees his intimate friend, and it is said to him: "Look at what so-and-so is suffering."

(Yubassarunahum) is the present tense of basarahu bi-l-amr, meaning he made him see it, that is, made him a viewer of it. Its origin is yubassaruna bihim, so the preposition was dropped and the verb was made to take a direct object.

The two pronouns refer to (hamimun, "intimate friend") in the nominative and to (hamiman, "intimate friend") in the accusative. That is, every intimate friend sees his intimate friend. The two pronouns are plural, in view of the generality of (hamimun) and (hamiman) in a negative context.

(Yawaddu) means he loves, that is, he wishes. This may happen through a thought that comes to his mind on seeing the punishment, or through a statement that issues from him, like His saying ﴿and the disbeliever will say: "Would that I were dust!"﴾ [al-Naba': 40]. This is the apparent meaning, that is, the disbeliever will cry out on that day and say: "I would ransom myself from the punishment with my sons, my spouse and my kin," and this will be a disgrace for him that day before his family.

Al-mujrim is one who commits a jurm, which is a great sin, namely disbelief, because at the beginning of the mission people were of two kinds: disbelievers and obedient believers.

(Yawma'idhin, "that day") is the same as ﴿the day the sky will be like molten metal﴾. If His saying ﴿the day the sky will be﴾ is linked to (yawaddu), then His saying (yawma'idhin) is an emphasis of ﴿the day the sky will be like molten metal﴾. If it is linked to His saying (ta'ruju al-malaikatu, "the angels ascend"), then His saying (yawma'idhin) conveys that this day is the day when the guilty one would wish to ransom himself from punishment with those mentioned after it.

[Page 161]

(Law, "would that") is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), so what follows it is in the position of the object of (yawaddu), that is: the day of ransoming oneself from punishment with his sons, and so on to the end of the verse.

Al-Jumhur read (yawmi'idhin) with a kasra on the mim of (yawm), in the genitive, by the annexation of (adhab, "punishment") to it. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha on the mim, as its being built on the annexation of (yawm) to (idh), which is an indeclinable noun. Both readings are permissible.

Al-iftida' means giving a ransom (fida'), which is what is given as a substitute for rescue from a consequence. From it is His saying ﴿and if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85] in al-Baqarah, and His saying ﴿even if he were to ransom himself with it﴾ in Al 'Imran. The meaning is: would that he ransom himself. The preposition (bi-) after the root of ransom introduces the substitute given, so the meaning of (bi-) is substitution.

The meaning of (min, "from") is figurative origin, since the verb (yaftadi, "ransoms himself") is taken to mean (yatakhallasu, "frees himself"). (Sahibatuhu, "his spouse") means his wife.

Al-fasilah (kin) means the nearest relatives of the tribe, and they are the relatives who are separated from one, that is, those who are extracted from one. So it includes fathers and mothers. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Ashhab said: "I asked Malik about the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿and his kin who shelters him﴾, and he said: 'It is his mother.'" Meaning: the father is understood from it by the way of implication (lahn al-khitab, what is understood from the implied sense of the speech). So the nearest kin are fully mentioned, both explicitly and by implication. As for the well-known interpretation, al-fasilah indicates the fathers by the wording, and the mothers are derived by the implication of the discourse.

The relatives have been arranged according to the degree of natural inclination towards them in common custom, because natural inclination arises from constant companionship and frequent association.

He did not mention the two parents, because they are included in al-fasilah, for the sake of brevity.

Al-iwa' means gathering together and taking refuge. He, exalted is He, said ﴿he took his brother to himself﴾ [Yusuf: 69], and He said ﴿I will take refuge in a mountain﴾ [Hud: 43].

As for (allati tu'wihi, "who shelters him"): if it means the tribe, then al-iwa' is a figurative usage for protection and support, that is, and despite that he would ransom himself with them, knowing that they will not avail him anything that day. If it means the mother, then al-iwa' is in its literal sense, with regard to the past tense and the present-tense form, to bring the state vividly before the mind, like His saying ﴿and Allah is He who sends the winds, so they raise clouds﴾ [Fatir: 9]. That is: he would wish to ransom himself with his mother, despite the strength of his attachment to her, since she used to shelter him.
