For this reason, giving testimony, when the witness is asked for it, is obligatory upon him, as He said: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

Upholding testimony is attending to it and preserving it until it is given. This is a figurative uprightness, as was discussed earlier with His saying (﴿and who establish the prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]) in the sura of al-Baqarah.

The **ba'** in **bi-shahadatihim** is for accompaniment, meaning they stand accompanied by the testimony, and the meaning of the particle becomes, through metaphor, the meaning of transitivity.

So mentioning uprightness in testimony completes the traits of the people of Islam, and it does not require a counterpart among the traits of the people of polytheism mentioned earlier.

So **al-muhafazah** refers to completing the pillars of prayer, its conditions, and its times. The choice of the present-tense verb is to indicate the renewal of that guarding and the absence of negligence in it. By this you know that this sentence is not merely an emphasis of ﴿who are constant in their prayer﴾, but rather it carries an additional meaning, while the purpose of emphasis is achieved by repeating what indicates their care for prayer in both sentences.

Among the prophetic reports are many reports about the virtue of prayer and that the prayers expiate sins, such as the hadith: "Do you know what his prayer achieved?" [Page 175] Between the last of these prayers and the first there is the rhetorical embellishment of **radd al-ajuz 'ala al-sadr** (the return of the final element onto the beginning).

The placement of the subject before the verbal predicate in His saying ﴿And who are attentive to their prayer﴾ indicates the strengthening of the predicate, with the renewal indicated by the present-tense verb.

Since these noble attributes were ascribed to them, their reward for them was reported: that they are honoured in Paradise.

This is an **istithna' munqati'** (a disconnected exception) arising from the threat that begins with His saying ﴿The guilty one would wish to ransom himself from the punishment of that Day﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 11], and so on.

He turned away from naming them by the description "Muslims" to enumerating some of their qualities, as **itnab** (elaboration) in praising them, because the context of praise calls for elaboration, and to draw attention to the fact that each of these eight attributes is among the causes of dwelling in the gardens.

Some of them may be found among the polytheists, but they do not observe them fully and consistently, and that is the keeping of trusts and covenants. The polytheist keeps a trust and a covenant in order to avoid the blame of betrayal and treachery, and he keeps them with his allies but not with his enemies. The polytheist testifies to the truth when he has no desire to lie and when he fears being branded a liar. The polytheists betrayed the Muslims on several occasions, and some of them betrayed others. So if a polytheist knew that no one would discover his lie, and he had a desire for it, he would not give his testimony.

The placement of the subject before the verbal predicate in His saying ﴿And who are attentive to their prayer﴾ indicates the strengthening of the predicate, with the renewal indicated by the present-tense verb.

Since these noble attributes were ascribed to them, their reward for them was reported: that they are honoured in Paradise.

The demonstrative pronoun was used to draw attention to the fact that they deserved what follows the demonstrative because of what preceded it, as discussed in His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] in the sura of al-Baqarah.

**Al-ikram** is honour and good reception, meaning that together with their reward of the bliss of the gardens, they are honoured with good welcome and praise. He said: ﴿The angels will enter upon them from every gate: "Peace be upon you, for that you endured patiently; excellent is the final abode"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23–24], and He said: ﴿And the good pleasure of God is greater﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72].

This requires that His saying **fi jannat** (in gardens) be a predicate of the demonstrative pronoun, and His saying **mukramun** (honoured) be a second predicate.

﴿Then what is the matter with those who disbelieve, rushing toward you, ﴾36﴿from the right and from the left, in groups?﴾37﴿Does every one of them aspire to be admitted into a Garden of bliss?﴾38﴿No!﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 36–38]

This is a rhetorical question expressing denial and wonder at the gathering of the polytheists around the Prophet (ﷺ), mocking what they heard of the promise of Paradise for the believers and the threat of the torment of Hell for the polytheists.

This follows from what was stated in His words, ﴿Those will be in Gardens, honored﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 35].

The meaning is: the disbelievers have no hope of entering Paradise, so why do they try, by gathering around you with the signs of their mockery?

Although this is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), its intended audience is the disbelievers, to whom he conveys what is recited to them from the Qur'an. In meaning, it is directed at them, as indicated by its being introduced with the particle of deterrence, so it is not appropriate that it be informing the Prophet (ﷺ) of this, since it is a matter already established in his knowledge.

The meaning of ﴿So what is the matter with those who disbelieve?﴾ is: what state has befallen those who disbelieve while they are in your presence, or while they are hastening toward you?

This was mentioned previously at His words, ﴿They said, "And why should we not fight in the cause of Allah while we have been expelled from our homes?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246], in Surat al-Baqarah. The construction *ma lahu* (what is to him) cannot be free of either a single circumstantial element (*hal*, a circumstantial accusative) or a clause after the interrogative which is the target of the question. So it is permissible that the circumstance toward which the question is directed here be the adverbial phrase *qibalaka* (before you), meaning that it is a settled adverbial (*zarf mustaqarr*), and the bearer of the circumstance is *lil-ladhina kafaru* (to those who disbelieve). It is also permissible that *muhti'in* (hastening) be the circumstance, in which case *qibalaka* is a loose adverbial (*zarf laghw*) attached to *muhti'in*. On both possibilities, both are the object of wonder regarding their state, so whichever of them is made the locus of wonder, the other is treated in the manner suitable to it within the construction. In the Mushaf, the *lam* attached to *alladhina* is written separated from what follows it, which is a rare orthography.

*Al-Ihti'a'* (hastening) is extending the neck while walking, as was mentioned previously at His words, ﴿Hastening toward the caller﴾ [al-Qamar: 8], in Surat al-Qamar.

Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn 'Atiyya and the author of al-Kashshaf said: The polytheists used to gather around the Prophet (ﷺ), listen to his words, deny him, and mock the believers, saying, "If these people enter Paradise as Muhammad says, we will surely enter it before them, and we will have in it more than they have." So Allah revealed this verse.

*Qibal* is a noun meaning *'inda* (in the presence of).

The placing of the adverbial phrase before *muhti'in* is for the sake of emphasis, because the wonder at their state in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ) is stronger, given the impudence that is in them.

The position of His words, ﴿from the right and from the left﴾, is like the position of *qibalaka* and the position of *muhti'in*. The intended meaning is multiplicity of directions, i.e., coming toward you from every side.

The definiteness in *al-yamin* and *al-shimal* is the definiteness of the genus, or the *alif-lam* is a substitute for the genitive complement (that is, what would have been said after them, meaning "from your right and from your left").

The intended meaning of mentioning the right and the left is the encompassing of all directions, so the right and the left were mentioned alone because they are the two directions around which one is typically surrounded. Similar to this is the verse of Qatari ibn al-Fuja'a:

*Indeed, I see myself as a target for the spears, at times from my right, and at times in front of me.*

He means: from every direction.

*'Izin* is a circumstantial element (*hal*) of *alladhina kafaru*. *'Izin* is the plural of *'izah*, with the *z* lightened, and it means a group of people. It is a noun of the pattern *fi'ah*. Its original form was *'izwah*, of the pattern *kiswah*, and not of the pattern *'iddah*. The plural of *'izah* followed the analogy of the sound masculine plural without regular justification, and it is from the category of *sanah*: every triliteral noun whose final radical was deleted and compensated for by the *ta' marbuta*, and which was not broken into a plural, like *'idhah* (meaning "a piece").

This construction in His words, ﴿So what is the matter with those who disbelieve, before you, hastening﴾ up to His words, ﴿a Garden of bliss﴾, may be a figurative allegorical image (*isti'arah tamthiliyyah*), in which their state of rushing toward the Prophet (ﷺ) is likened to the state of those who are thought to be gathering in search of guidance and attainment, seeking forgiveness in order to enter Paradise, because the norm is that none gather around the Prophet (ﷺ) except those seeking guidance by his way.

On this view, the interrogative is used in its original meaning, because the allegorical image operates over the whole discourse while its individual words remain in their literal senses.

It is also possible that the discourse is an interrogative used to express wonder at their state of rushing, then their denial and mockery.

The sentence ﴿Does every one of them aspire to be admitted into a Garden of bliss?﴾ is a comprehensive substitution (*badal ishtimal*) from the sentence ﴿So what is the matter with those who disbelieve, before you, hastening﴾ up to the verse, because their gathering around the Prophet (ﷺ) is, by its nature, for seeking guidance and salvation. Thus their state is likened to the state of those seeking salvation and guidance, and an interrogative is directed at it.

The exegetes relate that the polytheists said, mocking: "We will enter Paradise before the Muslims." So it is permissible that the interrogative be a denial of their pretense of hope for Paradise, by taking their mockery in a sense contrary to what they intended, by way of the wise mode of discourse (*al-uslub al-hakim*, indirect speech that responds to an opponent in a manner other than his expectation), or by expressing the pretense of hope through the verb *yat'am* (aspire), as in His words, ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down upon them informing them of what is in their hearts﴾ [al-Tawbah: 64], meaning: they pretend that they fear.

The attribution of the hope to *kullu imri'in minhum* (every one of them), instead of saying, "Do they aspire to enter Paradise?", is a depiction of their state as the state of a group in which each one wants to enter Paradise, because they are equal in this, each of them seeing himself as equal in it. So in His words, *kullu imri'in minhum*, there is a strengthening of the mockery directed at them.

Then, built upon the mockery, there follows what nullifies what was assumed for their state, by the deterrent particle that the allegorical mockery is built upon, namely *kalla* (No!), meaning: that will not be. This is a transition from the figurative to the literal, and from mocking them to rebuking them, to preempt the thought of one who imagines that the preceding speech was not mockery.

Here the discourse is complete regarding the affirmation of the reward.

This is a new statement that begins a fresh topic (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a resumptive sentence that opens a new subject), used to move from affirming the requital to arguing for the possibility of resurrection, in refutation of their doubt that drives them to deny it. That denial was mentioned briefly in His earlier words (*Indeed, they see it as far off, but We see it as near*). So He argued against them from the first creation, as He said, ﴿And you have already known the first creation, so why do you not remember?﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 62]. The statement ﴿Indeed, We created them from that which they know﴾ is therefore used to imply its necessary meaning, which is the affirmation of the re-creation of their bodies after their annihilation.

This is part of the continuing address directed to the Prophet ﷺ, and its purpose is that it should reach the ears of the polytheists, as was mentioned just before.

The meaning is: We created man from a drop of semen until he became a rational human being capable of debate, and in the same way We will re-create him in a manner they do not know.

What is referred to by ﴿that which they know﴾ is what everyone knows, namely that he was formed in his mother's womb from a drop and then a clinging clot. But they knew this first creation, and their familiarity with it distracted them from reflecting on its indication of the possibility of re-creating what was formed from it by another formation.

[p. 179]

He deviated from saying "Indeed, We created them from a drop," as He said in other verses, ﴿Indeed, We created man from a drop of mingled fluid﴾ [al-Insan: 2], and ﴿Does man not see that We created him from a drop, and then he is a clear adversary?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 77], and ﴿And he presents for Us an example and forgets his creation. He says, "Who will give life to bones while they are decayed?"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 78], and other numerous verses. Instead, He used the relative form in His words *that which they know*, as a means of directing mockery at them, since they argued and were obstinate, while knowledge of what they were disputing exists within themselves though they are unaware of it. Among this is His saying, ﴿And you have already known the first creation, so why do you not remember?﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 62].

In His words *that which they know* there is also an allusion that they will be created in a second creation from that which they do not know, as He said in another verse, ﴿Glory be to He who created all the pairs from what the earth grows, and from themselves, and from that which they do not know﴾ [Ya-Sin: 36], and He said, ﴿And We will produce you in what you do not know﴾. So there was in the first creation a secret that they do not know.

The emphatic particle *inna* is used with *khalaqnahum* in order to treat them, in respect of the false doubt they expressed, as though they did not know that they were created from a drop and were non-existent. How, then, do they deem impossible the re-creation of their form after some of its parts have perished and some remain? Then He followed this allusion to the possibility of re-creation with an explicit statement in His words ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests that We are indeed able﴾ ﴿to replace them with better than them﴾, as a consequence of His words ﴿Indeed, We created them from that which they know﴾. The implied sense is: "Then indeed We are able," and so on.

The clause ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts﴾ and what follows is a parenthetical insertion between the *fa* (so) and what it introduces.

Swearing by God through the attribute of His lordship over the easts and wests means His lordship over the whole world, because the world is confined to the directions of the sun's rising and setting.

The plural *al-mashariq wa al-maghareb* (the easts and the wests) is used in consideration of the multiplicity of the sun's risings and settings across the seasons of the year, for this is a wondrous manifestation of the divine power and the lordly wisdom, since it indicates the magnificent craftsmanship of God in that it points to the movements surrounding the sun, which is among the greatest of created things. For this reason, no oath is mentioned in the Qur'an by a direction other than east and west, rather than north and south, even though north and south are two well-known directions among the Arabs. God swore by them in accordance with the customary way of the Qur'an's oaths.

In choosing the easts and wests to be sworn by in the attribute of their Lord, there is observance of the appropriateness of the sun's rising after its setting, as a figure for life after death.

[p. 180]

The discussion of the particle of negation with *la uqsimu* has already been given at His words ﴿So I do not swear by what you see﴾ and ﴿nor by what you do not see﴾ [al-Haqqah: 38–39] in Surat al-Haqqah, and at His words ﴿So I do not swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 75] in Surat al-Waqi'a.

His words ﴿to replace them with better than them﴾ allow two meanings. The first, which suits the context, is that the meaning is: to replace them with something better than them, that is, to replace their very selves with a creation better than the creation they are upon today. The superiority lies in perfection, swiftness, and the like. It was a creation more perfected than the first creation, because it is suited to the world of eternity, whereas the first creation was suited to the world of change and perishing. On this understanding, *nubaddila* (We replace) is used with the implied meaning of *nu'awwid* (We compensate), and the first object of *nubaddila* is a pronoun like the pronoun in *minhum* (from them), namely *nubaddilahum* (We replace them), and the second object is *khayran minhum* (better than them).

*Min* here is comparative, meaning "better in creation," and the comparison is made in view of the difference between the time of the first creation and the second creation, or the difference between their two worlds.

The second meaning is: that We replace these people with something better than them, that is, with a nation better than them, and the superiority lies in faith. On this understanding, *nubaddila* keeps its original meaning, and its object is omitted as in the first meaning, and *khayran* is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, namely the *ba'* of substitution, as in His words ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61]. **Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 70, verses 42–44:**

﴿So leave them to plunge in vain talk and play until they meet their Day which they are promised.﴾ ﴿The Day they emerge from the graves hastening, as if rushing to a shrine.﴾ ﴿Their eyes downcast, humiliation covering them. That is the Day they were promised.﴾

This is a consequence of what is implied in His saying: ﴿So what is wrong with those who disbelieve, racing toward you﴾ (al-Ma'arij: 36). That is, their intention, shown by their conduct and their saying, "We will enter the Garden," was to mock the Qur'an and the Prophet (ﷺ). After refuting this in general and in detail, the command of God to His Messenger to leave them follows, since He knows that guidance and argument have not benefited them, and that they persist in obstinacy and hostility.

The meaning of the command to leave, in His saying ﴿fa-dharhum﴾ ("so leave them"), is a command to disregard what preoccupied the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding their obstinacy and their persistence in disbelief, despite the clarity of the proofs for the Resurrection. Since the greatest cause of their turning away and their persistence in disbelief was their plunging and playing, the Qur'an uses this as a metonym for turning away, saying ﴿yakhuduu wa yal'abuu﴾ ("they plunge and they play").

Thus the phrase ﴿yakhuduu﴾ and the phrase ﴿wa yal'abuu﴾ are two circumstantial clauses (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in ﴿fa-dharhum﴾. This circumstance is a restriction on the command in ﴿fa-dharhum﴾. The implied sense is: "Leave their plunging and their play, and do not grieve over their obstinacy and persistence."

The verb ﴿dhar﴾ ("leave") is transitively linked to the pronoun ﴿hum﴾ ("them") in the manner of attributing an act to the entity itself, meaning that the act is directed to one of its particular states that are specifically relevant to that act. Examples include His saying ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ (al-Ma'ida: 3), meaning that eating it is forbidden to you, and His saying ﴿and [forbidden is] that you combine two sisters﴾ (al-Nisa': 23), meaning that you combine them together in a marriage bond. Reliance in this is on the contextual indication, as in the two verses mentioned. Also His saying in Surah al-Tur: ﴿So leave them until they meet their Day in which they will be struck senseless﴾ (al-Tur: 45). Or, it depends on mention of something indicating a particular state, as in His saying ﴿yakhuduu wa yal'abuu﴾ in this verse. In such cases the implied object may differ, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows are an abomination from the work of Satan, so avoid it﴾ (al-Ma'ida: 90). The implied meaning is: "Avoid drinking intoxicants, gambling for stakes, worshipping idolatrous altars, and seeking decisions by divining arrows."

This usage is what the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) classify under attributing permissibility and prohibition to the entities themselves, or ascribing prohibition and permissibility to entities. Because the indication of this usage on the intended meaning is clear, the majority of scholars of usul do not count it among the ambiguous (mujmal) forms, unlike al-Karkhi and some Shafi'is.

The command to leave may also be used as a figurative means of expressing contempt and indifference, like the words of Kabsha, sister of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib, urging her brother 'Amr to avenge their brother 'Abd Allah, who had been killed:

*Leave 'Amr alone, for 'Amr is at peace,*
*Is the belly of 'Amr more than a span for a meal?*

The same style is found in this verse. That is: "Do not care about them, for they are too insignificant for you to turn your resolve to their affair," like His saying: ﴿So do not let yourself be consumed in grief over them﴾ (Fatir: 8).

From this you learn that His saying ﴿fa-dharhum﴾ has no connection with the ruling on fighting, nor is it a truce, nor is it abrogated by the verses of the sword, as some commentators (mufassirun) have imagined.

*Khawd* means much talk, and the intended meaning is their plunging into talk about the Qur'an, the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Muslims.

*La'ib* means jest and mockery. It is their play in receiving the Islamic call, and their departure from the bounds of reason and seriousness in the matter, out of envy, rage, and fury, which has disturbed their sound judgment.

The verb ﴿yakhuduu﴾ and ﴿yal'abuu﴾ are in the jussive mood as the answer to the command, to emphasize the linking of their plunging and playing with the lack of concern for them. The implied sense of the jussive in the answer is: "Leave them, and they will plunge and play," that is, they will continue in their plunging and playing, and that will not harm you. Similar jussives are frequent, such as His saying: ﴿Tell those who believe to forgive those who do not expect the Days of God, so that He may recompense a people for what they have earned﴾ (al-Jathiya: 14), and His saying: ﴿And tell My servants to say that which is best﴾ (al-Isra': 53). Some commentators and grammarians take such jussives as governed by an implied jussive particle of command (lam al-amr), on the basis that this is a quoted speech, and this conveys the subtle point of emphasis.

[p. 183]

The phrase ﴿ḥattā﴾ ("until") is connected to ﴿fa-dharhum﴾, because it contains the sense of "give them respite and wait for them," for the Day they were promised is the Day of Resurrection, when they will be recompensed for their mockery and disbelief. So it does not serve as an endpoint for ﴿yakhuduu wa yal'abuu﴾. The endpoint here is a metonym for the continuation of leaving them.

The attribution of ﴿yawm﴾ ("day") to the pronoun ﴿hum﴾ is due to the slightest connection between them.

The majority recited ﴿yulaqqū﴾ with an alif after the lam, from *mulaqah* (encountering). Abu Ja'far recited it without the alif, from *liqa'* (meeting).

*Liqa'* is a metaphor under every reading. According to the reading of the majority, it is a metaphor in two respects, since the Day neither encounters nor is encountered. According to the reading of Abu Ja'far, it is a metaphor in one respect only, since encounter occurs only between beings.

﴿The Day they emerge from the graves﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿their Day﴾, not an adverbial of time (zarf).

*Khuruj* (emergence) is the appearance of their bodies from the earth.

The majority recited ﴿yakhrujūna﴾ with a fatha on the initial yā' as an active verb. Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited it with a ḍamma as a passive verb.

*Ajdath* is the plural of *jadath*, with two fathas, and it is the grave. The grave is a pit made to conceal the dead body.

The pronoun in ﴿yakhrujūna﴾ refers to the polytheists mentioned in the preceding reports. All of them were buried in graves or placed in the well of Badr.

*Nasb*, with a fatha and then a sukun, is an idol. It is also said *nuṣub* with two ḍammas. The reason it is called *nuṣub* is that it is set up for worship. al-A'sha said:

*And the set-up idol, do not worship it,*
*and do not worship Satan; worship God alone.*

﴿Yūfiḍūna﴾ is the present tense of *awfaḍa*, meaning to hasten and run in one's walk. That is, "as if they were going to an idol." Their hastening on the Day of Resurrection toward the gathering is compared to their hastening in the world toward the idols to visit them, since this hastening is specific to them. In this comparison there is an incidental inclusion (idmāj) serving to make their state in idol worship appear more dreadful, and an allusion to the fact that their hastening on the Day of Resurrection is a hastening of being driven and pushed, as a recompense for their hastening to the idols.

[p. 184]

The majority recited ﴿nuṣbin﴾ with a fatha on the nūn and sukun on the ṣād. Ibn 'Amir and Hafs, from 'Asim, recited it with ḍammas on the nūn and the ṣād.

The lowering of the eyes (*khushu' al-abṣar*) is a metaphor for looking downward out of humiliation, as He said: ﴿They look sidelong, with a furtive glance﴾ (al-Shura: 45), and He said: ﴿With lowered eyes they will emerge from the graves as if they were scattered locusts﴾ (al-Qamar: 7). The origin of *khushu'* is the manifestation of obedience or fear in a person.

*Rahaq* is covering, that is, being overtaken by something that conceals. Here it is a metaphor, since humiliation does not cover.

The clause ﴿That is the Day they were promised﴾ is a concluding summary (fadhlaka) of what the surah contained at the beginning of its themes, from His saying ﴿of a punishment about to occur﴾ (al-Ma'arij: 1) to His saying ﴿on a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ (al-Ma'arij: 4), and the verses that follow. It also conveys, together with that, the emphasis of the clause ﴿until they meet their Day which they are promised﴾. It also contains the rhetorical device of *radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr* (repeating the end of a phrase at the beginning of the next).

[p. 185]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah Nuh

This surah is called by this name in the codices and in books of tafsir. Al-Bukhari, in the Book of Tafsir of his Sahih, titled it "Surah *Inna arsalna Nuhan*" (Surah: "Indeed, We sent Nuh," Nuh: 1). Perhaps this was common in the speech of the early generations (al-salaf). al-Tirmidhi did not give it a title in his Jami'.

It is Meccan by consensus.

It is counted as the seventy-third in the order of the revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after forty verses of Surah al-Nahl were revealed, and before Surah al-Tur.

The counters in Medina and Mecca counted its verses as thirty. The people of Basra and Syria counted it as twenty-nine verses, and the people of Kufa counted it as twenty-eight verses.

* * *

**Its themes**

The greatest aim of the surah is to set forth as an example to the polytheists the people of Nuh, who were the first polytheists

[p. 186]

upon whom a punishment in this world was inflicted, namely the greatest punishment, which is the Flood. In this there is an illustration of the state of the Prophet (ﷺ) with his people, through their state.

It contains extensive detail about the call of Nuh (peace be upon him) to the oneness of God and the rejection of idol worship, his warning to his people of a painful punishment, his argument for them from the marvels of God's creation, and his reminding them of the Day of Resurrection.

It also contains the obstinacy of his people in disobeying him, and their firmness in their polytheism.

It names the idols they used to worship.

It contains Nuh's prayer against his people for their annihilation.

It alludes to the Flood.

It contains Nuh's prayer for forgiveness for himself and for the believers, and for the destruction of all the disbelievers.

Interwoven throughout is the incidental inclusion of the promise to the obedient of abundant provision, increase of offspring, and the bliss of the Garden.
